events.t: Closing the finance gap for regenerative agriculture
events.o: CA4SH, Landscape Alliance (ICRAF), Food and Land Use Coalition, The Rockefeller Foundation, YOUNGO, WBCSD, Clim-Eat
events.x: Transforming global food systems to deliver healthy diets, resilient livelihoods, and a sustainable planet requires a fundamental shift in how we manage agricultural landscapes. Regenerative agriculture offers an important pathway to achieving this transformation by restoring soil health, enhancing biodiversity, strengthening ecosystem function, and improving the resilience and productivity of agricultural systems. However, despite growing global momentum, the adoption and scaling of regenerative agriculture remains constrained by fragmented evidence, financial barriers, and policies that do not adequately support farmers and other actors through the transition.

events.t: Financing the Belém Health Action Plan: Launch of the BHAP Financing Framework
events.o: Brazilian Ministry of Health, WHO, Wellcome Trust, The Rockefeller Foundation
events.x: Climate change is increasingly testing the capacity of health systems to protect populations, maintain essential services and respond to evolving risks. Extreme heat and other climate-related hazards, changing patterns of climate-sensitive diseases, deteriorating air quality, and threats to food and water security are intensifying existing health challenges and creating new ones. Advancing dynamic, resilient and climate-ready health systems is therefore essential to protect health, safeguard development gains and ensure that countries can anticipate, prepare for and respond to climate-related impacts. This requires sustained political ambition, coordinated action across sectors and institutions, and financing that matches the scale and urgency of implementation needs.

events.t: Solution & Delivery AG 16. Accelerating Climate-Resilient Health Systems: Implementing Solutions and Reporting on Results of adaptation and mitigation actions in the sector
events.o: Health Care Without Harm, Race to Zero, Health Care Climate Challenge
events.x: This 60-minute showcase highlights concrete progress, measurable outcomes, and practical solutions for accelerating climate-resilient healthcare, serving as a status check on key health sector climate initiatives. Convening national health ministries, multilateral organizations, private health systems, civil society, funders, and technical partners, the event demonstrates how joint commitments under the Belém Health Action Plan (BHAP), the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health (ATACH), and Health Care Without Harm’s Health Care Climate Challenge and Race to Zero for Healthcare —supported by the new Global Green and Healthy Hospitals (GGHH+) framework—are driving actionable change. These efforts are actively monitored and reported in alignment with COP30 Key Objective 16 (Promoting Resilient Health Systems) and COP31 Priority: Dynamic and Resilient Health Systems.

ICAO: UN Decade of Sustainable Transport: Accelerating Sustainable Aviation Through UN System Synergies
events.sp: High-level speakers representing UN agencies and international organizations such as ICAO, UN Tourism, and, subject to invitation and confirmation, UN DESA, UNEP, the Clean Energy Ministerial (CEM), and the International Transport Forum (ITF), alongside representatives from industry.
events.x: This side event will highlight how international aviation is contributing to environmental protection and sustainable development as the UN Decade of Sustainable Transport (2026-2035) begins. Discussions will explore progress toward ICAO’s long-term global aspirational goal of net-zero carbon emissions by 2050, including advances in aviation cleaner energy and the implementation of the ICAO Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA). The event will also examine how aviation is addressing broader environmental challenges through partnerships across the UN system and with key stakeholders, while identifying opportunities to strengthen collaboration and accelerate collective action toward a more sustainable and resilient future for aviation.

events.t: Powering Cement's Net Zero Future: Scaling Renewable Energy for Industrial Decarbonization

events.x: Achieving net-zero cement and concrete requires a fundamental transformation of industrial energy systems. While alternative fuels, clinker reduction and carbon capture remain essential pathways, access to affordable and reliable renewable electricity is increasingly important for cement producers worldwide. The sector is accelerating renewable energy deployment through: On-site renewable generation Utility-scale solar and wind projects Corporate Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) Energy storage solutions Digital energy management systems Electrification of production processes Closer collaboration among industry, policymakers, energy providers and financial institutions is needed to unlock investment, improve enabling infrastructure and scale deployment.

events.t: Delivering SDG 11.2 Connecting Housing, Public Transport and Climate Action for Sustainable Cities
events.x: Public transport is not only a mobility solution. It is a climate, housing and urban development solution that can accelerate progress across multiple SDGs while supporting the objectives of the UN Decade of Sustainable Transport and the Paris Agreement. With only a few years remaining to achieve the SDGs, access to safe, affordable and sustainable public transport remains still out of reach for nearly 40% of the world's urban population. This session will launch the latest insights on SDG 11.2 and explore how integrated transport, housing and urban planning policies can accelerate climate action while creating more inclusive, resilient and liveable cities. Building on evidence from global SDG monitoring and practical city experiences, the organisations behind this paper, ICLEI, UITP and UN-Habitat, will discuss how transit-oriented development, integrated mobility planning, digitalisation and data-driven solutions and innovative financing mechanisms can improve accessibility and reduce emissions. The session will furthermore specifically explore how digital tools, data and innovation can support better mobility planning, improve public transport services, strengthen multimodal integration and enable more efficient and inclusive urban mobility systems, drawing on practical experiences from initiatives such as the IKI-funded ACCESS project, implemented in Latin America. The session will also highlight opportunities offered by the United Nations Decade of Sustainable Transport (2026-2035) as a framework for accelerating progress toward sustainable urban mobility and climate goals.

events.t: Transforming Waste Into Purpose: From Landfill to Cement Kilns
events.sp: Kevin Lunney, Cement Operations Director, Cimsa-Mannok; Soumya Chaturvedula, Director, ICLEI South Asia; Canan Derinöz Gencel, Director of the Environment and Climate Change Department, Turkish Cement Manufacturers Association (TÜRKÇİMENTO); Galip Tekiner, Chairman of the Board of Directors, TAYÇED
events.x: Every year the world generates over 11 billion tonnes of waste. Managing this growing waste stream is one of our biggest global challenges. Co-processing in the cement industry is a solution that transforms ‘non-recyclable’ waste into purpose. Instead of being sent to landfill sites, or dumped in streets, rivers and oceans – the waste can be collected and managed. In cement kilns, non-recyclable waste can replace fossil fuels as a source of energy, while its mineral content can be recovered and used as a raw material in cement production. This turns waste that would otherwise have little value into a useful resource. Despite its potential, greater use of co-processing is being held back by regulatory barriers, insufficient policy incentives, and gaps in waste collection, sorting and pre-processing infrastructure. In this session, we will examine global best practices for scaling up co-processing, while exploring the cross-regional challenges to scale up co-processing.

events.t: Launch of the CNT Catalogue of Sustainable Practices – Automotive Recycling
Low Carbon, High Resilience: Can Concrete Deliver Both?
events.sp: Berrak Erbuğa Avcioğlu, Çimsa; Ariana Karamallis, Build Change; Chris Williamson, RIBA; Zeynep Başaran, Chair of the Department of Civil Engineering, Özyeğin University
events.x: Construction plays an important part in net-zero transition. Tomorrow’s climate-resilient cities, coastal defences, clean power networks and digital infrastructure will all rely on concrete. That’s why low-carbon cement and concrete must sit at the heart of this transition. This session will explore: How low-carbon cement and concrete can help deliver climate-resilient cities and infrastructure capable of withstanding increasingly frequent and severe climate impacts while supporting global decarbonisation goals. It will position concrete not simply as a construction material, but as a resilient solution that provides durability, long service life, flood resistance, thermal performance and the ability to maintain critical services and infrastructure under changing climate conditions. How resilience and decarbonisation can be advanced together through the design and construction of buildings and infrastructure using low-carbon cement and concrete solutions. How these principles can be reflected in national climate policies, including Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) and National Adaptation Plans (NAPs). While climate mitigation strategies have traditionally focused on reducing emissions, there is a growing need for climate plans to also address the resilience and performance of the infrastructure being built today. NDCs and NAPs can support this by promoting resilient and low-carbon infrastructure, incorporating resilience criteria into public procurement, strengthening building codes and infrastructure standards, encouraging whole-life carbon assessments, and recognising the role of durable materials in reducing long-term climate and economic risks. Aligned with COP31's Climate-Resilient Cities, Resilient Infrastructure and Standards, and Climate Implementation Bridge agendas, the session will highlight the need for governments to integrate resilience and decarbonisation objectives within planning, financing and infrastructure delivery frameworks.

events.x: The panel will explore the transition towards low-carbon cement and concrete, with particular emphasis on the role of public policies in accelerating this transformation. Discussions will highlight the contribution of clinker substitution, supplementary cementitious materials (SCMs), blended cements, circular economy practices and innovative technologies to reducing carbon emissions. Furthermore, Türkiye's Green Cement Communiqué, which promotes the use of low-carbon cement, will be presented as a concrete example of market transformation driven by public policy. The discussion will also address practical experiences, implementation challenges and potential solutions for advancing a sustainable, climate-resilient built environment.

Strengthening Multilevel Financial Architectures for Subnational Climate Action
events.o: FMDV, Global Alliance of Subnational Development Banks, AMUF, CHAMP
events.x: Closing the subnational climate finance gap requires structural change in how finance is governed, channelled and deployed. Subnational governments hold public mandates, assets, revenues and investment responsibilities essential to national climate ambition. Strengthening their financial capacity can expand countries’ investment potential, mobilise domestic resources and translate international support into lasting development outcomes. This requires adequate, predictable resources and financial architectures that give subnational governments meaningful roles in shaping investment priorities, accessing finance and directing implementation.

events.t: Acting for a just transition: climate, development, jobs and investment
Beyond the Baku to Belém Roadmap to 1.3T
events.x: Official development assistance fell by 23.1 per cent in 2025, the largest annual contraction on record, while the New Collective Quantified Goal calls for climate finance to developing countries to reach at least USD 1.3 trillion a year by 2035. The gap between those two facts is the subject of this session. It asks what Africa should put on the table at COP32 in Addis Ababa to turn the Baku to Belém Roadmap into measurable delivery: more finance, at better terms, directed to the sectors that matter most. It is built as a candid exchange on the cost and terms of capital rather than a further round of pledges, and it closes by asking each institution present to name one commitment it will make between Antalya and Addis Ababa.

events.t: Carbon Has a Price. Who Finances the Transition?
events.x: Carbon is increasingly becoming a cost of doing business, but the rules, exposure and ability to finance the transition vary significantly across geographies. This session explores how carbon pricing, CBAM, emissions trading and evolving trade frameworks are reshaping the economics of cement and other energy-intensive industries across Europe, Türkiye, West Africa and other emerging and export-oriented markets. The discussion will examine how regions with different regulatory frameworks, energy systems, capital costs and access to technology can remain competitive while financing deep decarbonisation. From CCUS and electrification to calcined clay, alternative fuels, renewable energy and other low-carbon technologies, the panel will address the investment gap between climate ambition and industrial reality — and the role of green finance, development finance, carbon revenues, incentives and risk-sharing mechanisms in turning transition roadmaps into investable projects.

events.t: Global Campaign to Demand Climate Justice (DCJ)
Global Goals, Local Action: Powering the Transition in the Global South
events.x: EMDEs will play a decisive role in the global transition to net zero. Much of the world’s future population growth, urbanisation and infrastructure development will take place across the Global South, driving significant growth in demand for cement and concrete. These materials will be essential to building housing, transport networks, energy infrastructure, industrial facilities and climate-resilient cities. Ensuring that this new infrastructure is built with increasingly low-carbon cement and concrete will therefore be critical to keeping global climate goals within reach. While global climate goals provide an important direction of travel, there is no single pathway to decarbonisation. The transition must reflect local realities and development needs. The challenge is not just to reduce emissions from existing cement production, but to create the conditions in which low-carbon cement and concrete can become commercially viable and competitive as these markets grow. The session will focus on: Translating global net-zero goals into national decarbonsiation Identifying the most effective decarbonisation pathways for different EMDE contexts. Scaling commercially available solutions The policy frameworks, financing mechanisms and partnerships needed to translate global goals into locally tailored decarbonisation pathways in EMDEs How we can better align national climate commitments with cement and concrete decarbonisation pathways while supporting competitiveness, economic development and infrastructure growth

events.sp: Erdem Erdoğan, Finance and Financial Affairs Vice President, Çimsa
events.x: The net zero transformation of the cement sector can be accelerated not only by improving existing operations, but also by jointly developing breakthrough technologies, bankable project portfolios, resilient construction solutions and workforce capabilities. The event focuses on how roadmaps, financing mechanisms and bankable project portfolios can be implemented to support Türkiye’s low-carbon cement transition. The main axis of the event includes: EBRD’s role in Türkiye’s industrial decarbonisation The financing and coordination platform that TIDIP can provide for the cement sector The contribution of the MAF programme to Türkiye’s cement sector in terms of technical assistance, pilot projects and policy framework support The financial feasibility of decarbonisation investments from the perspective of a company CFO The development of implementation partnerships among public authorities, financial institutions and sector actors

events.x: Jobs and skills now decide whether the climate transition delivers. Workforce readiness determines whether projects reach financial close, whether committed capital is deployed and which economies keep the industries the transition creates. The transition could generate around 375 million net new jobs over the next decade across energy, construction, manufacturing and agriculture (Systemiq and WRI, Jobs and Skills for the New Economy, 2025), yet demand for green talent is growing at twice the rate of supply (LinkedIn, Global Green Skills Report, 2024). Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), where most delivery happens, have the least capacity to close this gap on their own.

events.t: Congressional Dialogue on Climate Mobility
Creating Lead Markets: From Climate Policy to Action
events.x: Technologies to decarbonise cement and concrete are available today and more are moving towards commercial deployment. However, scaling these solutions requires more than innovation alone. Companies need confidence that markets will reward lower-carbon products and support investment in new production capacity, alternative materials, energy systems and carbon capture technologies. We will explore how governments, industry, investors and buyers can work together to create lead markets for low-carbon cement and concrete. The discussion will focus on what has worked, where implementation gaps remain, and how public and private demand can be combined to accelerate deployment.

events.t: Scaling Sustainability Solutions • Building and Financing the Climate Capital Collaborative
Solution & Delivery AG 7. Implementing Ocean-Climate Action: Advancing the Marine Conservation Breakthroughs
events.o: Mangrove Breakthrough, Coral Breakthrough, Seagrass Breakthrough, Saltmarsh Breakthrough, Kelp Breakthrough, Seaweed Breakthrough
events.x: Marine conservation is essential to advancing and scaling ocean-based climate action. The protection, conservation and restoration of marine and coastal ecosystems—including kelp forests, mangroves, coral reefs, seagrass meadows and salt marshes—can make a significant contribution to achieving the long-term goals of the Paris Agreement. Beyond the capacity of coastal wetlands (mangroves, seagrasses, and saltmarshes) to store and sequester carbon, these ecosystems deliver critical benefits for people and nature. They support food security and livelihoods, protect biodiversity, and act as natural buffers against coastal erosion and the impacts of extreme weather events.

events.t: COP 31 Priority Spotlight - Oceans and Seas: Delivering and Powering Resilient Coastal Destinations - Mobilising investment and coordinated action through the Coastal Tourism and Ocean Renewable Energy Breakthroughs
events.o: Coastal Tourism Breakthrough, Ocean Renewable Energy Breakthrough
events.x: COP31 meets in Antalya, at the heart of one of the world's leading coastal tourism regions. Coastal and marine tourism accounts for around half of global tourism, generating some USD 1.5 trillion in direct GDP in 2023 (USD 3.3 trillion and 100 million jobs when supply chains are included) and around 3% of global greenhouse gas emissions. It depends directly on healthy coasts and seas, and its destinations sit on the front line of sea-level rise, erosion, coral bleaching and extreme weather.

events.x: At COP30 in Belém, governments recognized, for the first time in a UNFCCC decision, the land rights and traditional knowledge of Indigenous Peoples as part of climate action. They also made unprecedented commitments to deliver on that recognition. Through the Intergovernmental Land Tenure Commitment (ILTC), tropical forest countries committed to recognize and strengthen the land rights of Indigenous Peoples, Afro-descendant Peoples, and local communities across 160 million hectares by 2030. Funders renewed the US$1.8 billion Forest and Land Tenure Pledge, and the Tropical Forest Forever Facility committed at least 20% of its payments to Indigenous Peoples and local communities.

COP 31 Priority Spotlight - Rio Synergy: Three COPs, One Agenda: Closing the Data Gap Behind Rio Convention Delivery
events.x: COP31 closes a year of three separate COPs, in three countries, on three closely linked issues: land degradation, biodiversity loss and climate change. Governments rarely lack commitments on these issues. What they lack is a way to see how those commitments interact. Policies addressing climate, biodiversity and land are often designed in separate ministries and tracked through separate processes, so conflicts only become visible once they are expensive to fix, investments can undermine each other and synergies are missed, with the costs falling on communities. IPBES estimates USD 10 to 25 trillion a year in unaccounted costs from siloed approaches to biodiversity, water, food, health and climate (IPBES Nexus Assessment). Policy coherence is already recognised as a means of implementation for all SDGs under target 17.14 (UN SDG metadata); the gap is practical tools, not recognition. This Priority Spotlight Event, under COP31 Presidency priority 9 (Rio Synergy), looks at how open, connected and continuously updated policy data can help governments and their advisers see where climate, nature and land commitments align, where they conflict, and where one planning or implementation process could serve several Conventions at once, so that the policies that protect ecosystems also support healthy and thriving societies.
